hits.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 3 Abstract Background: The prevalence of depression among college students has significantly increased in the past decade. Depression is twice as common among college students than compared to the general population. Without early identification and treatment of depression, it can negatively impact important outcomes such as social connectedness, academic performance, academic retention, and future economic productivity. Objective: Early identification and depression screening should be a priority among the college population. The purpose of this quality improvement project was to develop an evidence-based Depression Screening Protocol for an identified college health center utilizing the patient health questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) and the patient health questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) integrated in the electronic medical record. Various meetings with the healthcare providers, directors, and staff were held to share rationale for the development of the depression screening protocol and helped to identify the questions and concerns regarding implementation of the Depression Screening protocol. Results: Of the college students receiving health services at the identified college health center, a total of 1,741 college students were screened for depression, 1,719 students completed the PHQ- 2, 22 students completed the PHQ-9, and 13 students were referred to counseling and psychological services. Conclusion: The Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) project demonstrated that the implementation of an evidence-based Depression Screening Protocol at a college health center was manageable and sustainable. This quality improvement project was successfully integrated into the identified health college center and it improved early identification of depression among college students.

Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified. Clinical Question In college-aged students (P), how does screening for depression with the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) (I) compared to current practice (C) affect early identification of depression (O)?

hits.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015). Ethics and dissemination The Ethics Committee of the Hamburg Medical Association approved the study. A clinical trial company will ensure data safety, monitoring and supervision. The multicentre GET.FEEDBACK.GP RCT is the first trial in primary care that tests the efficacy of a patient- targeted feedback intervention as an adjunct to depression screening. Its results have the potential to influence future depression guidelines and will be disseminated in scientific as well as patient- friendly language. Trial registration number NCT03988985.
